title: Phantom Codes: Hardness, Rate Optimal qLDPC Constructions, and Distance Limits
authors: Rui Mao, Weixiao Sun, Shengyu Zhang
abstract: An $[[n,k,d]]$ stabilizer code is phantom if every in-block logical CNOT gate can be realized by a permutation of its physical qubits. This eliminates the large and complicated physical overhead normally required for logical entangling gates. Yet this symmetry is highly restrictive: phantom codes are rare, the number of logical qubits is limited to $k=O(\log n)$, and no phantom qLDPC family with growing logical dimension was previously known.   We make three contributions.   1. We prove that recognizing phantomness of a given stabilizer code is at least as hard as Graph Isomorphism, even for CSS codes encoding only $k=2$ logical qubits.   2. We propose the first rate optimal phantom qLDPC families: for every fixed $D$, our CSS families achieve the maximal logical scaling $k=Θ(\log n)$ and distance $d\geq D$.   3. We prove a distance no-go theorem: every phantom code family with $k=ω(\sqrt{\log n})$ and check weight $w=O(1)$ satisfies $d\leq w$ for sufficiently large $n$.   Thus our fixed-distance qLDPC families are distance-scaling optimal at the maximal logical scaling $k=Θ(\log n)$.
summary: This paper studies 'phantom codes,' a rare class of quantum error-correcting codes with special symmetry properties. The authors establish that determining if a code is phantom is computationally hard (GI-hard) and provide constructions for optimal families. Crucially, they prove a distance limit, showing that for codes with high logical dimension relative to their check weight, the distance must be severely constrained.
main_problem: Characterizing 'phantom codes,' which are stabilizer codes where all logical CNOT gates can be realized by physical qubit permutations, and determining the inherent limitations on their parameters.
main_result: The authors proved that recognizing phantomness is as hard as Graph Isomorphism, constructed rate-optimal phantom qLDPC families, and established a distance no-go theorem for such codes.
method: The work combines algebraic coding theory (stabilizer codes, CSS codes) with computational complexity theory (Graph Isomorphism reduction) and group theory (automorphism groups).
model_or_system: The model is the stabilizer code, specifically CSS codes, defined by their parameters $(n, k, d)$ and analyzed via their automorphism groups $	ext{PAut}(S)$.
key_observables: Code parameters: physical length ($n$), logical dimension ($k$), distance ($d$), and check weight ($w$).
important_parameters: The scaling of $k$ relative to $n$ (e.g., $k = \Theta(\log n)$ or $k = \omega(\sqrt{\log n})$) is critical for the theorems.
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes the code is a binary CSS code and relies on the structure of the automorphism group action on the logical Pauli group.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the phantom property, then proving the computational hardness (GI-hardness), followed by constructing optimal qLDPC families, and concluding with the distance no-go theorem.
why_interesting: The connection between the algebraic structure of quantum error-correcting codes and computational complexity (GI) provides deep insights into the inherent limitations of quantum information processing.
